headline: A Twente–ASML team moved the top of a lithography wafer support pillar 9.3 nanometres using a 4.5-micrometre piezoelectric film beneath it, the first active substrate support built from thin films rather than bulk actuators, which is what makes thousands per clamp conceivable.

items.title: A wafer support pillar that pushes back, 9 nanometres at a time
items.dek: A University of Twente and ASML team built a lithography wafer support whose pillars sit on a 4.5-micrometre film of lead zirconate titanate, a ceramic that deforms under voltage, and moved a pillar top 9.3 nanometres — the first active wafer support made from thin films instead of bulk actuators.
items.why_it_matters: Height error in the clamp is the one focus term a scanner cannot chase. The levelling system measures the field and tilts to it, so tilt and slow curvature get corrected; error that changes from one contact point to the next, at millimetre spacing inside a single exposure field, survives into the printed image. Making each contact point individually commandable converts that residual from a machining tolerance fixed at manufacture into something adjustable per wafer.
items.background_md: Projection lithography prints only while the image plane stays inside the resist, and Rayleigh's criterion sets that tolerance at k₂λ/NA² — a budget that shrinks with the square of numerical aperture. Wafer bow, film stress, layer topography and the clamp itself all draw on it. A scanner does not press the wafer against a continuous flat surface: it rests on thousands of small raised projections called burls, because a contaminant particle then falls between them instead of dimpling the wafer, and because burl tips are easier to machine into one plane than a whole slab is.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is a 4.5 µm Pb(Zr₀.₅₂Ti₀.₄₈)O₃ film between LaNiO₃ electrodes, under a 3 × 3 array of octagonal silicon pillars on a 7 × 7 mm test piece; the octagon comes from the crystallographic etch selectivity, not from a design choice. Displacement was read with an aixACCT double-beam laser interferometer at three stages of the build: 20 nm on the bare electrode/piezo stack, 19 nm once the isolation layer was added, and 9.3 nm at the pillar top with 267 kV/cm applied.

The gap is the interesting part. Finite-element modelling predicts 21 nm at the pillar top, and the authors attribute the shortfall to leakage through pinholes in the isolation layer — the same leakage that held the drive field below the 300 kV/cm they wanted. They also report the bonding and isolation layers peeling near the centre of the device. Nothing here is a scanner result: it is a nine-pillar proof of principle at 7 mm, against a clamp that needs thousands of pillars, per-pillar wiring and a controller that knows what each one should do.

glossary.definition: One of the thousands of small raised projections on a lithography wafer clamp; the wafer rests only on their tips, so a stray particle falls into the gap between them rather than deforming the wafer.

The total range of focus a process tolerates while linewidth, sidewall angle and resist loss stay in specification; Rayleigh's paraxial form is k₂λ/NA², so it falls as the square of numerical aperture.
Lead zirconate titanate, a ferroelectric ceramic whose lattice distorts under an applied electric field; here a 4.5 µm film of it supplies the pillar's motion.
Electric field strength inside the film, which is what a piezoelectric responds to rather than the raw applied voltage; this device was driven at up to 267 kV/cm.

items.fab_angle: MNF's stepper meets the same budget from the other end. With a passive chuck there is no correction path at all, so the flatness error is whatever the wafer and the chuck already have — which makes measuring the club's actual focus range, rather than estimating it, the useful first move.

items.title: Analog compute costs 13 fJ; holding the transistors still costs 3,000×
items.dek: Christof Teuscher of Portland State laid out an analog computing cell in SkyWater's open 130-nanometre process and found that the four bipolar transistors doing the arithmetic spend 13 femtojoules per evaluation while the complete cell spends 39.6 picojoules — about 3,000 times more, none of it on computing.
items.why_it_matters: Analog accelerator proposals are almost always costed at the primitive: the exponential a junction gives you for free, the sum a wire gives you for free. This layout puts a number on what has to surround it — servo amplifiers holding operating points draw 74.5 percent of the supply current and the bias network another 22 percent — which says the thing to optimise in an analog fabric is composability rather than the operation. Sharing amplifiers across cells recovers roughly two of the three orders and still loses.
items.background_md: A bipolar junction's collector current is exponential in its base–emitter voltage, and Kirchhoff's current law sums currents at a node with no hardware at all. That pairing is why analog computing keeps returning: functions that cost a digital datapath many gates and many cycles fall out of device physics in one step. The standing objection is not the operation but everything around it — an analog value has to be held at an operating point, made addressable, and calibrated, and each of those needs circuitry whose cost does not shrink when the primitive does.
items.deeper_md:
The primitive is eml(x, y) = exp(x) − ln(y), which Odrzywołek showed in March 2026 generates the scientific-calculator basis from the constant 1 by composition alone. Four junctions evaluate it: the exponential and the logarithm come from Boltzmann statistics across the base–emitter junction, the subtraction from a current-summing node. That core is 13 fJ and 2.7 percent of the cell's area, and beats a width-matched digital datapath by 4× to 134× across the sensitivity sweep.

Then the cell: 39.6 pJ, about 3,046× the core. Extracted non-idealities cost 2.6× when an interior node must hold a specific value and essentially nothing — 0.95× — when it only has to be repeatable, so the penalty is the scaffolding rather than the operator. A second limit is grammatical rather than electrical: closure over the reals excludes trigonometry, and 18 of 100 surveyed physics equations need an irreducible trigonometric factor. The caveat the paper states itself, unusually plainly, is that no part has come back from fabrication and no number in it is a measurement of a physical device; everything is simulation and post-layout extraction.

glossary.definition: The two-input function exp(x) − ln(y). With the constant 1, composing it generates the arithmetic, algebraic and transcendental functions of a scientific calculator, which is why it was tried as a single analog primitive.
Femtojoule and picojoule, 10⁻¹⁵ and 10⁻¹² joules of energy per evaluation; the factor of a thousand between the two numbers quoted here is the entire finding.
A feedback amplifier whose job is to hold a node at a commanded voltage or current rather than to compute anything; in this cell it is where 74.5 percent of the supply current goes.

SkyWater's open-source 0.13 µm CMOS process design kit, which ships models for free NPN and PNP bipolar devices alongside its MOSFETs, so a layout like this one can be extracted and repeated by anyone.

items.fab_angle: The whole result is in SKY130, which is the PDK a student tapeout would actually use, and it leans on the free NPN devices that come with the deep n-well rather than on a paid bipolar option — so the layout and the extraction are reproducible with the open PDK and a SPICE simulator.

items.title: An input-only analog pin that talks back, at 10 kilobits a second
items.dek: A Rochester Institute of Technology group fabricated a 55-nanometre heart-rate sensor front end in which 39 square micrometres of added transistors shift the amplifier's input offset with data, turning a pin that is meant only to receive a signal into an outbound channel readable from outside the package.
items.why_it_matters: Analog front ends are signed off on gain, bandwidth and noise, and all three specifications are still met while the channel is running — the measured cost to the sensor output is 0.03 decibels of signal-to-noise ratio. The property being violated has no test because nobody writes it down: which direction a pin carries information. That makes pin directionality something a specification has to assert and a test has to check, the way pin voltage limits already are.
items.background_md: A mixed-signal front end is the circuit between a sensor and an analog-to-digital converter: an amplifier, a filter, and enough bias circuitry to keep both in their linear range. Its input pin connects to the amplifier's summing node, which is deliberately made high-impedance so the sensor's small current is not loaded down. High impedance cuts both ways. A node that draws almost no current also moves easily, so whatever voltage the amplifier develops at its own input appears on the package pin as well, with nothing in between to stop it.
items.deeper_md:
The payload switches extra transistor fingers into the transimpedance amplifier's differential pair, so the input-referred offset becomes a function of the data bit; feedback drives the amplifier's input node to that offset, and the node is the pin the sensor is wired to. Three conditions must hold: a closed-loop amplifier, its input exposed on a pin, and input impedance high enough that the injected offset is not shunted away. The added circuitry is 39.284 µm² in commercial 55-nm CMOS, under 0.001 percent of a typical biosensing front end and small against the 0.0049 mm² this one occupies, and the front end keeps its three gain settings from 12.25 to 140 mV/µA.

The stealth claim is where to push back. Worst-case perturbation is 5.9 percent against 34.3 percent of natural process and temperature spread, so it hides inside variation — but the 256-bit pseudorandom message was recovered error-free only at 6 bits per second. The 10 kb/s figure is a ceiling with raw SINR below −20 dB, lifted above 14 dB by filtering that already knows what to look for, and every measurement was taken at room temperature.

glossary.definition: An amplifier that converts a current into a voltage, used wherever the sensor is a current source such as a photodiode; feedback holds its input node at a fixed potential.
The small DC error an amplifier behaves as though it had at its input, set by mismatch between the transistors in its differential pair; switching extra fingers in and out changes it on command.
Signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio in decibels. The covert signal sits below −20 dB raw, which is why an attacker who knows the modulation can read it and an oscilloscope on the pin cannot.
Photoplethysmography, the optical pulse measurement in a watch or pulse oximeter: an LED lights tissue and a photodiode current is read out, which is why its front end is a transimpedance amplifier.

items.title: A GPU instruction word is 128 bits; the operands average 42
items.dek: Two Tsinghua researchers reverse-engineered the bit layout of NVIDIA's native GPU instruction set and re-synthesised it with a constraint solver, cutting the instruction footprint of 142 Blackwell kernels by 33 percent — the fixed 128-bit container carries operand and modifier fields averaging about 42 bits.
items.why_it_matters: Instruction supply is a bandwidth problem before it is a decode problem: every bit of the container has to be fetched from memory and held in the instruction cache whether or not it means anything. Shrinking the container buys instruction-cache capacity at no algorithmic cost — the added fetch and decode logic here is about nine times smaller than the instruction-SRAM bit-cell area it saves — and it puts a number on how much of a shipped GPU front end is layout convention rather than necessity.
items.background_md: A GPU's native instruction set is not the CUDA or PTX a programmer writes; it is SASS, the binary the hardware decodes, and NVIDIA does not document its encoding. Instructions sit in fixed-width containers, which makes fetch and decode simple: the next instruction always begins at a known offset, and a field lives in the same bit positions for every opcode that has it. The cost is paid twice — a short instruction is stored at the width of the longest one, and any field that appears at several different positions needs a multiplexer per position.
items.deeper_md:
Two results come out of one slot-assignment formulation over 975 instruction forms. Keep the 128-bit container and only move fields, so each field name is extracted from as few positions as possible: multiplexer count falls from 1,202 to 121, decoder area by 16 percent and power by 21 percent against the observed NVIDIA layout. Allow a variable-length 64/96/128-bit pipeline instead and instruction footprint falls 33 percent on 142 Blackwell kernels, 33.1 percent on Hopper and 29.6 percent on Ampere. The synthesised fetch/decode frontend closes 1.5 GHz in TSMC 22 nm and adds roughly 1,913 µm² per subcore, which the authors put at 0.12 percent of a GA100-class die.

The encoding underneath all of it is recovered, not documented. A generated disassembler agrees with NVIDIA's own nvdisasm on instruction identity and field values across 3.78 million instructions spanning four generations — strong evidence the recovered layout is right, and still not a statement about what NVIDIA's decoder does internally. The area accounting excludes cache tags and peripheral logic, and control-flow-correct handling of the scheduling control bits would need branch-merge resets the paper does not build.

glossary.definition: The native binary instruction encoding an NVIDIA GPU decodes, one level below PTX; it is undocumented and changes between architecture generations, so its layout is recovered by disassembling compiled code.

A constraint-programming solver that finds an assignment satisfying hard constraints while minimising an objective; here it places instruction fields into bit positions without letting co-occurring fields overlap.
How many selectors a decoder needs to pull fields out of an instruction word. It falls when a field always sits in the same bit positions, and it tracks decoder area and power directly.

NVIDIA's own disassembler for compiled GPU binaries, shipped with the CUDA toolkit; it prints SASS for architectures through Blackwell and is the ground truth a reverse-engineered decoder gets checked against.

items.title: The same MXFP4 pipeline written seven ways, and hand-RTL is not smallest
items.dek: Three European researchers implemented one 12-stage MXFP4 block dot product — the four-bit block floating-point multiply under edge AI inference — seven times, once in hand-written SystemVerilog and six times in hardware construction languages, and every generated version matched or undercut the hand-written one on FPGA area.
items.why_it_matters: Comparisons between hardware languages normally change the design along with the language, so what gets measured is the designer. Holding the microarchitecture fixed — same pipeline depth, same initiation interval, same part, same toolchain — separates the two, and what survives is that elaborating a circuit out of Scala, Python or Haskell does not cost silicon: the SpinalHDL entry is 206 source lines against 705, using 8,602 lookup tables against 11,025.
items.background_md: Register-transfer-level design in Verilog or VHDL describes a circuit directly: every wire, register and multiplexer is written out by hand. A hardware construction language instead runs a program — in Scala, Python or Haskell — whose output is that circuit, so loops, type parameters and higher-order functions become circuit generators rather than simulated behaviour. What comes out is still ordinary RTL, and the language never sees a transistor. The open question has always been whether that indirection leaves anything on the table once a synthesis tool has finished with the result.
items.deeper_md:
The fixed design is a 12-stage, initiation-interval-1 pipeline for an OCP MXFP4 block dot product — exponent selection, quantisation, multiply-and-sum, conversion back to FP32 — closed at 100 MHz on a Xilinx Artix-7 xc7a100t in Vivado 2025.1. Against 705 source lines and 11,025 LUTs for SystemVerilog: Chisel 298 lines and 10,846 LUTs, SpinalHDL 206 and 8,602, Amaranth 255 and 9,096, Clash 290 and 7,361, Bluespec 281 and 7,333. C++ through Vitis HLS is the outlier at 11,662 LUTs and 11,059 flip-flops.

One confound sits in the table and is worth naming: Clash and Bluespec also consumed 46 and 32 DSP blocks, mapping multiplies into hard multipliers the other flows left in fabric, so their LUT column is not like-for-like against the rest. The authors state the other limits themselves — one kernel, one device, one toolchain — and 100 MHz is a loose constraint that every synthesised entry met with positive slack between 0.135 and 0.307 ns, so nothing here is a timing-limited comparison either.

glossary.definition: The OCP microscaling four-bit float: 32 elements in E2M1 form share one 8-bit E8M0 exponent scale, so the block spans an FP32 exponent range while each element carries one sign, two exponent and one mantissa bit.
A pipeline that accepts a new input every clock cycle. Fixing it holds throughput constant across all seven implementations, so the comparison is about area and timing alone.
The lookup table, an FPGA's basic logic element — a small programmable truth table. LUT count is how FPGA area is counted, the way gate count works for an ASIC.

The step where a hardware construction language executes its host program to emit a netlist or Verilog; none of the host program's control flow survives into the circuit except the structure it built.

items.title: Write the GPU kernel sequentially, let the compiler prove the barriers
items.dek: Three MIT researchers built Exo-GPU, a language in which a CUDA kernel is written as ordinary sequential code and the parallel loops and barriers are annotations on it, so a compiler can check that the parallel version computes what the sequential one says — and the matrix-multiply kernels that result pass 80 percent of an H100's peak.
items.why_it_matters: On a Hopper-class GPU the programmer, not the hardware, is responsible for overlapping data movement with arithmetic, which means placing arrive and await pairs by hand around asynchronous tensor-core and memory operations. Those are the bugs testing does not find: a missing barrier is a race that produces a wrong number under one occupancy and the right one under another. Making the sequential reading the specification gives a mechanical answer to whether a synchronisation is sufficient.
items.background_md: A compiler for a conventional CPU decides for itself which loops to vectorise and when to prefetch, and it is usually right. Accelerator kernels invert that: the schedule — tiling, staging through shared memory, which warps do what — is where nearly all the performance lives, and it is too workload-specific for a compiler to infer. User-schedulable languages split the difference by separating the algorithm, written once, from a script of rewrites applied to it, with each rewrite obliged to preserve meaning. The compiler stops choosing and starts checking.
items.deeper_md:
The design decision is that parallelism carries no semantics. A program means what its sequential reading means; `cuda_tasks` loops and barrier annotations only say which threads execute which statements and where synchronisation restores that reading. Checking then splits in two: Exo's existing rewrite rules — the paper counts more than sixty verified transformations — preserve sequential meaning through scheduling, and an Abstract Machine interpretation checks that the parallel annotations do not change it. The language exposes the Hopper machinery directly, with TMA bulk copies and multicast, mbarrier arrive/await pairs, wgmma, distributed shared memory across CTAs, and warp specialisation with per-warp register counts.

The limits are the authors' own. The Abstract Machine check runs on selected concrete problem sizes rather than symbolically, so it is a check on an instance rather than a proof for all shapes; shared-memory aliasing is conservative and the programmer cannot control lifetimes; and the `cuda_tasks` loop order is fixed lexicographic with round-robin assignment. The cuBLAS comparison is also unpinned — the claim is that the Exo-GPU kernels surpass it in some configurations, without naming which shapes.

glossary.definition: A shared-memory barrier object on NVIDIA GPUs from Hopper onward, split into an arrive and an await so a thread can launch an asynchronous copy, do other work, and only then block until it lands.
Hopper's warpgroup matrix-multiply-accumulate instruction: a whole warpgroup issues one asynchronous tensor-core operation, and the result cannot be read until a separate wait has completed.
Giving different warps inside a block different jobs — some only move data, some only compute — so the memory pipeline and the tensor cores stay busy at the same time.
The property Exo-GPU's checker establishes: that running the program top to bottom as written, and running it with its parallel annotations honoured, produce the same result.

items.title: PPO's critic learns a flat line, because its own loss asks for one
items.dek: A group spanning Shanghai Jiao Tong, Tsinghua, Shanghai AI Laboratory and four other institutions show that the value network in reinforcement learning for language models flattens out across a response, and that supervising it at only three well-separated token positions instead of every token lifts Qwen3-4B's maths average from 37.60 to 45.57 percent.
items.why_it_matters: Dense supervision looks free — there is a reward at the end, so why not regress every position against it? Writing the mean-squared error out shows what it costs: the loss separates into the error of the response's average predicted value plus the variance of the predictions within that response, so the second term is a standing penalty on the critic for distinguishing states at all. That is a property of the objective, not of the network, and it does not go away with more parameters.
items.background_md: Policy-gradient training of a language model needs a baseline: an estimate of how good a partial response already is, so an update can credit a token for improving on that estimate rather than for the final score alone. PPO learns the baseline with a second network, the critic, trained by regression against the observed return. Rewards in this setting arrive once, at the end of the response, so every intermediate position is regressed against the same terminal number — and the per-position signal has to be extracted from that.
items.deeper_md:
The diagnostic is to estimate each intermediate state's true value by sampling K independent continuations from it and averaging their terminal rewards, then compare how sharply that moves against how sharply the critic's prediction moves. The critic is far flatter, and flattens further as the state space grows: in a FrozenLake control experiment, predictions smooth out across grid cells as the maze gets larger.

Two causes are identified. The mean-squared critic loss over a response decomposes into the squared error of the mean prediction plus the within-response variance of the predictions, so dense supervision applies that variance penalty at every one of T positions. And adjacent states differ by one token, so their gradients are nearly aligned — the paper shows gradient similarity decaying with token distance, which makes dense supervision largely repeated updates. SP³O therefore supervises relative positions 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9 of each response, adding 0.95 past 6,144 tokens; three states beat sixteen and sixty-four, and fixed placement beat random. Qwen3-8B gains far less than Qwen3-4B, 48.50 to 50.51 percent against 37.60 to 45.57, and that shrinking margin is the number to watch.

glossary.definition: The second network PPO trains alongside the policy, predicting the expected final reward from a partial response; subtracting its prediction from the observed return gives the advantage the policy update uses.
The ground truth the critic is measured against here: sample K independent continuations from a given partial response under the current policy and average their final rewards.
The unit of a difference between two percentages. Moving from 37.60 to 45.57 percent is 7.97 pp, which is not the same as a 7.97 percent relative improvement.
A setting where the only reward arrives when the response ends, so nothing in the training signal distinguishes one intermediate state from another except what the critic infers.

foundations.topic: Depth of focus, and why the wafer has to be flat
foundations.subtitle: The wafer may be wrong in the vertical direction by tens of nanometres and no more, and that one number explains planarisation, wafer chucks, and half of a process flow.
foundations.tldr: Focus is not a setting, it is a budget. Rayleigh turned "the image is out of focus" into a phase error between diffracted orders and got a tolerance of roughly k₂λ/NA² — a distance that shrinks as the square of the lens's numerical aperture. Everything the wafer brings to the exposure, its bow, its film stress, its topography and the clamp beneath it, is spent out of that same distance.

sections.heading: The quarter wave that became a distance
sections.body_md: Start with what focus physically is. A lens gathers the light diffracted by the mask and converges it as a spherical wavefront; at best focus every ray arrives having travelled the same optical path, so the diffracted orders are in phase and interfere into the pattern you drew. Move the wafer a distance δ away from that plane and the rays stop agreeing. Mack's derivation writes the disagreement as an optical path difference, OPD = δ(1 − cos θ), where θ is the angle at which a ray leaves the exit pupil — zero at the centre of the pupil, largest at its edge. Rayleigh's move was to ask how much of that a pattern can absorb. If OPD reaches a quarter of the wavelength, the zeroth and first diffracted orders end up 90° out of phase and stop interfering altogether: there is no image at all, not a blurry one. So the tolerable OPD is written k₂λ/4 with k₂ < 1, and that inequality is the entire criterion.
sections.deeper_md: The quarter-wave figure is a limit, not a spec. It is the defocus at which contrast goes to zero for a three-beam image, so any usable process sits well inside it — which is exactly why k₂ is defined as a fraction less than one rather than computed. Rayleigh's original context was telescope resolution; the lithographic version swaps the star for a grating and the eye for a resist.

sections.heading: From a phase error to λ over NA squared
sections.body_md: Turning that into a distance needs the angles. For a grating of pitch p the diffracted orders leave at sin θ = mλ/p, so a fine pattern throws its first orders out to large angles and a coarse one keeps them near the axis. Expand the cosine for small angles, OPD ≈ ½δ sin²θ, substitute the quarter-wave limit, and the focus range comes out as DOF = k₂λ/sin²θ — which, rewritten in terms of pitch, is p²/λ. Small features do not merely have less depth of focus; they have quadratically less. Rayleigh then took the extreme case. The finest pitch a lens can pass puts the first order right at the edge of the pupil, where sin θ = NA, and that substitution gives the form everyone quotes: DOF = k₂λ/NA². Notice what was assumed to get there. The expression holds for a binary line-and-space pattern sitting at the resolution limit, with three beams through the lens, at a numerical aperture small enough that the higher Taylor terms could be discarded.
sections.deeper_md: Both Rayleigh scaling laws come from the same substitution and share the same weakness. Resolution goes as k₁λ/NA and DOF as k₂λ/NA², so halving the printed feature by doubling NA costs four times the focus range. That asymmetry, not the resolution gain, is what drove immersion, off-axis illumination, and eventually planarisation as separate lines of attack.

sections.heading: What the formula stops describing above NA 0.5
sections.body_md: Mack's own lecture notes put it bluntly: the paraxial Rayleigh form does not work for today's lithography. Three of its four assumptions fail at once on a modern tool. Numerical apertures passed 0.5 decades ago, so discarding the sin⁴ and sin⁶ terms is no longer allowed. Illumination is shaped rather than coherent, so two-beam imaging is common — and two-beam imaging is the least focus-sensitive case there is, which is the point of shaping the source. And production patterns sit above the resolution limit rather than on it. Keeping the exact OPD instead gives DOF = (k₂/2)·λ/(1 − cos θ), valid at any numerical aperture. Immersion falls out of the same algebra: fill the gap between lens and wafer with a fluid of refractive index n and every optical path is multiplied by n, so the tolerable defocus grows. The gain is at least the refractive index and more at fine pitch — for 193 nm light in water, n = 1.46, Mack's curve runs from about 1.5× at 550 nm pitch to 1.9× at 200 nm.
sections.deeper_md: The immersion ratio is DOF(immersion)/DOF(dry) = [1 − √(1 − (λ/p)²)] / [n − √(n² − (λ/p)²)]. As pitch grows the ratio tends to n; as pitch approaches the dry diffraction limit the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator and the ratio climbs. Immersion therefore helps most exactly where it is needed most, which is unusual and is why 193i lasted twenty years.

sections.heading: Nobody measures depth of focus with the formula
sections.body_md: In a fab, DOF is an experiment. You expose a grid of fields, stepping focus along one axis and dose along the other — a focus–exposure matrix — and then measure the resist. The profile is modelled as a trapezoid with three numbers: linewidth, sidewall angle, and resist loss relative to the coated thickness. Plot linewidth against focal position with one curve per dose and you have a Bossung plot, named for the Perkin-Elmer field engineer who published the characterisation in 1977. The curves are flat-bottomed near best focus and turn away at the edges. The reason the dose axis has to be there at all is that focus and exposure are coupled: as an image blurs, the image slope at the line edge falls, so a smaller dose error is enough to move the linewidth out of spec, and exposure latitude collapses as you move away from focus. Sidewall angle and resist loss can be plotted the same way, and often one of them fails before linewidth does.
sections.deeper_md: In Mack's simulated example the three responses fail in different places: the CD window is wide and shallow, the sidewall-angle window is narrow in dose and centred low, and the resist-loss window cuts in from one side of focus. The overall process window is the intersection, so the specification that dominates changes with the feature and the resist — which is why a DOF number without its three profile specifications is not a measurement.

sections.heading: The process window, and the rectangle you fit inside it
sections.body_md: Replot the matrix as contours — the two linewidths at the edges of specification, an 80° sidewall-angle contour, a 10 percent resist-loss contour — and the region where all three hold is the process window. It is a capability, not a number. To get a number you ask what range of focus and dose errors fits inside it, which means fitting the largest rectangle you can, and there is no unique answer: every maximum rectangle is a different trade of focus tolerance against dose tolerance, and asking for the maximum-area one is meaningless. Plot their heights against their widths and you get the curve that matters, exposure latitude versus depth of focus, sloping down to zero. Mack's worked example gives, for a 15 percent exposure-latitude requirement, 0.85 µm by the rectangle method and 1.14 µm by the ellipse method that treats errors as random rather than systematic; the average, 1.00 µm, is the honest figure. Quoting a DOF without its specifications and its exposure latitude is quoting nothing.
sections.deeper_md: Rectangles and ellipses bracket the truth rather than competing. A rectangle is the right shape for purely systematic errors, where the corners are reachable; an ellipse is a surface of constant probability for two random variables, so its corners are not, and it always fits larger. Real focus and dose error have both components, so the rectangle result is pessimistic, the ellipse optimistic, and the average is the usual metric. Mack also notes that quoting DOF as ± a distance is obsolete: focus behaviour for small features is asymmetric, so only the total range means anything.

sections.heading: Everything upstream is spending the same budget
sections.body_md: Now run it backwards. If a process has 1.0 µm of focus range, every source of vertical error shares it: lens field curvature, the levelling system's residual, resist thickness variation, the topography left by layers already built, the wafer's own bow, and the clamp it is pressed against. This is why planarisation stopped being optional — Mack names chemical mechanical polishing as a change that altered the nature of optical lithography precisely because it removes focus error. It is also why a scanner does not lay the wafer on a flat table. The wafer rests on thousands of small projections called burls, so that a stray particle falls between them instead of dimpling the wafer up into the image plane, and so that only the burl tips have to be machined into one plane. The floor keeps moving: the Twente and ASML work in today's Pulse is an attempt to steer individual support pillars at the 9-nanometre scale, which tells you how little of the budget is now left.
sections.deeper_md: Resolution follows directly from all of this, and Mack defines it that way: the smallest feature printable with a specified depth of focus. For i-line at NA 0.54 and σ 0.5, his simulation gives 0.33 µm if you require no focus range at all, 0.38 µm at 1.0 µm DOF, and 0.43 µm at 1.5 µm. Push it further and the NA scaling inverts — with 1 µm of DOF required, resolution is best at NA 0.59 and gets worse above it, because DOF falls off faster than resolution improves. Contacts are the worst feature type and isolated lines the most forgiving.

glossary.definition: The extra distance a ray travels relative to the ideal wavefront when the wafer is out of focus: δ(1 − cos θ) for defocus δ and pupil angle θ. It is a phase error expressed as a length, which is why the tolerance comes out in wavelengths.

The dimensionless factor in DOF = k₂λ/NA². It is not a constant of nature — it absorbs the illumination, the resist, the feature type and whatever specifications you are holding — and Rayleigh's derivation establishes only that it is less than 1.

Whether the zeroth order and both first orders reach the wafer, or only two beams do. Three-beam imaging is the most focus-sensitive case and the one Rayleigh's formula assumes; off-axis illumination deliberately arranges two-beam imaging to buy focus range back.

Linewidth against focal position, one curve per exposure dose, taken from a focus–exposure matrix. Named for John Bossung, who published the characterisation in 1977; the flat-bottomed region of a curve is the usable focus range at that dose.

The region of the focus–dose plane where linewidth, sidewall angle and resist loss are all in specification. It describes what the process can do; the largest rectangle or ellipse fitted inside it describes what the process is being asked to do.

The percentage dose variation a process tolerates while staying in specification. It trades directly against depth of focus — every extra point of latitude is bought with focus range — which is why neither number means anything quoted on its own.

One of the thousands of small raised projections on a lithography wafer clamp. The wafer contacts only their tips, which keeps total contact area to a few percent of the wafer, lets particles fall into the gaps, and reduces the flatness problem to machining the tips into one plane.

foundations.try_this: Run a focus–exposure matrix on the club's stepper. Expose one field per focus step across the widest range the stage will take, repeat the row at four or five doses, measure the resulting linewidths under the microscope, and plot linewidth against focal position with one curve per dose. That is a Bossung plot, and the width of the flat-bottomed region on the best curve is the depth of focus the process actually has. Do it before arguing about resolution: by Mack's 1997 definition, a resolution number quoted without the DOF it was measured at does not mean anything.
